## 3. The Kid Detective (2020)

**Score:** 35
**Body:** Oh what a dark little treat! I had been meaning to get to this for a long time. It's 90 ish minutes long, on Netflix right now. I'd call it a black comedy, it really is quite funny in parts. Compare it to Brick and The Nice Guys, although it's definitely darker and meaner than those, especially at the end.

Adam Brody is handed a big task, the movie lives and dies on what he can communicate to you in subtle ways, making his deteriorated state seem both pathetic but also just the right side of annoying. In what he chooses to conceal and reveal emotionally, he does a lot. 

Sophie Nélisse is also very good, I had only been familiar with her from Yellowjackets, she's in a role that could feel hectoring and unpleasant without her generosity. 

The epilogue is what really made me love this, when all the chips have fallen and we're left with a few minutes of aftermath, that's the moment the movie chooses to avoid the easy catharsis and it's better for it.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. The Exorcist (1973) still creeps me out

**Score:** 69
**Body:** I was just talking about it with a movie-buff that's not quite Gen Z but also not old enough to remember 9/11, and he shared a view that I've noticed in previous conversations with people that see "The Exorcist" under the influence of 'pop culture lore'.

They expect a scary, almost emotionally traumatizing experience, yet they pick apart the movie's technical achievements - the sound design, dubbing, and makeup that are doing major heavy-lifting in Linda Blair’s performance, all somewhat dated by today's standards - to say they were not scared by them. "It wasn't convincing enough, I wasn't fooled, I almost laughed".

But the unsettling feel of the picture - that still creeps me out, even though I also wasn't fooled by the effects when I got to watch the movie for the first time - doesn't come solely from believing there's a demon, or The Devil with capital D, possessing this girl. It comes from the girl being subjected to graphic medical procedures in the first half, or from being keenly aware of the normalcy that surround the events. Like, Ellen Burstyn was really just having a cup of tea downstairs while the priests performed the exorcism and all that crazy supernatural shit was going on in the house! 

Horror is a deeply subjective genre, and almost as time-stamped as comedy, but "The Exorcist" is one of those movies that I still find deeply unsettling regardless of how convincing the illusion still remains more than 50 years later.

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. What are these comments lol…

Yeah absolutely! I find it taps into the same horror that people find scary today in films like Obsession. This poor girl didn’t choose this, she’s still in there suffering during her possession, and that makes it even more painful for the mother who sees glimpses of her daughter in pain.

The movie also has a lot to say about belief. The mother never lets go of it, never stops believing that her daughter can be cured, no matter the costs. It’s that faith that ultimately saves her daughter at the end of the day. It’s the strongest belief that defeats evil in the end; Pure, unaltered faith that no matter what happens, evil can be overcame. Even if it comes at the expense of exhaustion, pain and even death.
2. Some bizarre comments here, think a few people being a bit contrarian and edgy for the sake of it. I love the Exorcist anyway but it stands on its own merits as a truly remarkable film. A deeply interesting portrayal of a crisis of faith, of which the horror is the sideshow to the core dilemma at the heart of the story.

It manages to leave a deep sense of unease after watching it, it’s a great film and I actually think it’s aged really well.
  - I was 17 when I watched it, in my best friend’s basement, with my volleyball team, after our final season. Turned into a crazy night and we were all pretty terrified. The movie stuck with me for a month.
3. It is my favorite film of all time. And for me, what’s changed over the years is that I am horrified less by the viscera that disturbed audiences so much in 1973 than the spiritual and emotional peril of Chris and Father Karras. A mother who doesn’t know how to help her daughter, a priest losing his faith in a broken world — those are fears I identify with more and more as I get older.

And then the strange triumph of the finale:

“Is she going to die?”

“… *No*.”

Chills every time.
4. The strength of The Exorcist is that it's a very well-rounded movie with a strong core narrative and themes, and excellent performances. When it opened in '73 the horror was infamously overwhelming (which the producers played into to create its reputation), but even if its scares are showing their age for younger audiences - and I'm not even sure that's true uniformly, but let's assume it is - it is still a powerful and disturbing story about loss of faith, redemption, and bodily violation. I think in a way its public reputation for stomach-churning terror belies its sombreness, and how good a film it really is
5. I watched the film at a very young age, and it had a really big impact on me. To this day, 25+ years later, I can't watch the film and look at her face without feeling dread and horror and turning myself away.
6. Recently I saw a Dahmer MKUltra video, which showed the scene from Exorcist III Dahmer would play to get in the mood, pretty much a monologue describing his own killings. Then it said the writer of the movie was some CIA guy working the "psychological warfare" department. Now that's actually creepy.
7. something that stuck out at me on a rewatch of the exorcist years ago was that the medical shit is probably scarier than the demonic possession stuff. they really nailed what it is to be a kid undergoing all these invasive medical tests, which is a real grounded kind of horror
8. To this day, it is the best American horror movie ever made. IMO opinion, nothing really comes close.

This, despite the fact that Friedkin said his intention was not to make a horror movie, but rather, one about "the mystery of faith"

## 2. Charles Kane from Citizen Kane (1941) has to be one of the best written characters in cinema

**Score:** 33
**Body:** I found the character arc of Charles Kane very compelling because it works on so many levels.

Since the movie covers almost every aspect of his life starting from back when he was a kid to him dying, every part of him is explored without sacrificing the pace or thematic elements of the film. I look at biopics that fail so often, trying to cover every part of the person’s life only to end looking like a montage sequence that reads like an informative Wikipedia article rather than trying to say something important. But Citizen Kane does not fall into this trap. The character of Charles Kane is embedded into this film’s masterpiece status. 

Perhaps the part of it has to do with the fact that it is told in a dynamic non-linear structure, which was a lightning in a bottle concept at that time and was executed to perfection. I would be dreading it if a character’s life were told in a non-linear structure normally, especially if I do not find the character interesting. Charles Kane has all of the qualities to be an interesting character. Film immediately establishes the chokehold he has on the real world (forget fantastical big guns; big guns set in the real world are a different gravy). The huge contrast between his status and the relatively insignificant thing that he longs for in his final moments just forces it to be an interesting mystery.

With every real-life consequence his close ones or the world sees/experiences, we see/learn something about his life adjacent to it. His character pops out like a sore thumb because he contradicts the people and ideas surrounding him at the moment, which makes his character arc hard to miss. The film lays out his ideals clearly in front of us (literally at one point), which makes it easy to read his character. The story is constructed in a way that it keeps the mystery engaging, progresses the themes naturally, and teaches about this character at a nice pace… all of his life. Because Charles and the world have so much synergy amongst each other (Charles Kane and his world are very vocal about each other), and Charles's ideals are like an open book, his actions make realistic sense, or at least they give off an illusion that they do.This is very important to me because I always feel like there is a hint of governance by the filmmaker shaping the character's actions but not Charles Kane, which is a big step to make a character feel like a real person. 

So basically Citizen Kane is goated and deserves all of its praise.

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. My favorite thing about Kane is that the entire enterprise is a failure. Kane fails at everything he attempts. His newspaper goes bankrupt, his political campaign fails, his marriages and personal friendships all fail. Even the reporter assigned to learn what "rosebud" means fails at his assignment.

The movie was even a failure at the box office. It was poorly-marketed and Hearst made sure it got bad reviews. Even Orson Welles became something of a failure in his later life after a brilliant early start.

Yet all this failure manages to produce one of the greatest films ever made. I feel like there's a lesson there.
  - I see your point about Welles’ career, and while he certainly did suffer a considerable blow being practically blacklisted after his initial contract, I do think calling him a failure in his later life ignores the considerable work he did with titles like F is for Fake or Chimes at Midnight.
    - Or Paul Masson wine. 
2. This is a bit undergrad film critic 101, but if you go down the list of top 250 movies (or memorable ones), they almost perfectly know how and when to play the trope, lampshade things etc. Citizen Kane is a great example because even when you know the trope, the flawed hero etc, it is still enjoyable to see how it is played. Using Rosebud and the non-linear structure means as a viewer you can go through the emotional journey of Kane. Posting Charles' ideals in a literal document might be tired in another setting, but for the newspaper and the story it feels compelling. 

*Jaws* is a good example. Structurally, it is almost absurdly classical. A threat appears, authorities refuse to acknowledge it, our protagonist is forced into action, a group of men goes into the wilderness to hunt the monster, and eventually the hero defeats it. Spielberg does not seem embarrassed by any of this. He plays the archetypes cleanly. But he is extremely precise about timing. You barely see the shark for much of the film. The conventional monster reveal is withheld. So the film gives you the structure you unconsciously expect while denying you the visual payoff until it matters. Even the shot choices MAXIMISE the tropes, like the ferry scene and the zoom in on the beach. 

The same with Kane. That shot of him and his wife in Xanadu vs the shot of him with his mum at the beginning. 
3. I watch a video the other day that talk about how Charles Kane seems so complex and real because the movie retains information from him. Some very important moments the light shadows his face so we cannt infer what he is really feeling. As a result one as an audience member has to fill that gap and "create" his own version of Kane. I think he really hit the nail on the head with that analysis and to me the best movies are the ones where the audience has an active rol in the story trying to understand the characters like Haneke's films.
4. I’m Still Here (2024) failed in this regard. The first 80 minutes or so were great but it fell apart in the end and should have been at least 30 minutes shorter. Shame, since it could have been a great biopic (which is kinda rare).
5. The scene of Charles finishing Leland’s review is one of the most important moments of character writing in cinema. It is where you find the last real parts of decency within him, that he was committed to the integrity of his press, when all other integrities had been abandoned by the end of the election.

## 3. There is no way Disney expected the Mandolorian to be a success. They just wanted to see toys

**Score:** 30
**Body:** Title edit: \*sell toys ;)

I've just finished watching the Mando movie after renting it on Youtube. It's actually worse than expected.

Starwars movies tend to always try to do a few things: 1. advance (or backfill for Solo and Rogue One) the universe, add to the lore by showing new things about Jedi, weapons, vehicules, alien races etc..., tell a cool story.

Narration: nothing actually happens in the end. No character growth, no impact on the world, no stakes.

Starwars lore contribution: close to zero except showing how the Hutt's fight (hint: like sausages). The new planets are bland in particular the weird 1950s America planet that just felt like a way to keep budget low.

Speaking of which: production value felt very low. From the costumes to the CGI backgrounds, it really felt like a TV show, or worse (Mando S1 looked like a million bucks). Jon Favreau, how did you get dragged into this?

Action: For a movie with two faceless protagonists (a helmet clad dude and a puppet), it was again, pretty bad, from Sigourney to the human villains to the Hutts.

Music and sound design: Move over John Williams! !The movie ends with a gipsy guitar / yiddish-musik version of the Mando theme. I'm actually not sure if it's a joke but I thought it was hilarious. Sound design ain't nothing to write about but again in this movie, absolutely nothing of note when Starwars all tended to massively contribute to modern sound design from lightsabers, to Tie fighters to the sonic charge to the thunder on Exegol (and it's also hard to find good point about the new trilogy).

... In conclusion: WTH Disney? It seems clear that the goal now is to produce "content" to sell toys. But I'm not sure until when consumers will follow forever (Grogu only seels because of Mando S1).

Last point: all cameos of Dave Filloni also felt super weird. Take a cue from Peter Jackson, it should be a quick "oh nice", not "oh... weird, why is this guy wearing a cowboy hat"

The end.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I mean Caravan of Courage and Battle for Endor have existed since the early days of the franchise. The bar is not very high for cheap looking movies adding nothing to the franchise. I think all the money was gone in paychecks.
  - Comparing ABC tv movies to a film released to paying customers is certainly a thing to do. 
    - Different medium and circumstances but same intent: a cash grab

Star Wars merchandise is a billion-dollar-a-year industry, and Grogu is their biggest seller by a large margin. the movie is meant to be a clean entry point and repeated rewatch for kids who are too young to sit through an entire series. the entire thing is a blatantly crass and cynical endeavor.

that said, the 10-15 mins of him and the Babu Friks going on a tiny adventure was really cute

I’m not sure what they expected globally but that’s where it tanked. Not sure how popular the character is outside of US.

I do think the film was largely a marketing strategy and a way to decrease the cost of a TV only release.

I also enjoyed it more than people were trying to tell me I would. 
  - It's 300 million they wouldn't have made if it was just Mando Season 4 as originally planned.

It feels like they're just sort of harvesting the franchise for parts and cash now, while praying that Starfighter is going to revitalize the fanbase - which it won't.

They updated Galaxy's Edge, they promoted at Burger King, and they just want to catch the wave on the 'impressions'. Disney is all about that long game. Vertically integrated, multimedia marketing.
5. Just watched it last night. I kept reading that it’s not terrible, it’s fun, etc. But seriously what the hell was that? 

Poorly scripted, poorly acted. It kept moving at a fast click, at least, and the shots of the X-wings and other ships at the beginning looked great. I also think Ludwig’s soundtrack just didn’t do much for me. 

I guess it’s for Mando fans and that’s it.

7. I’m afraid you’ve misunderstood the movie, and have some strange ideas about corporations, and have kind of a circular argument that seems to disprove itself.

“Star Wars movies always advance the lore” — I lean sure, sometimes, but it’s not like anyone sits down and says “one goal of this movie is to create newl lore”… that’s backwards. If the story they’re telling requires new lore, sure. The this movie’s failure to do what you assert all Star Wars movies do… well, to me that reads more like your assertion is wrong than some kind of defect in the movie.

And I really, really do not think Favreau or Felloni or others who worked on this movie tried to make a bad movie, or expected it to flop. That’s really not how movie making works. And certainly the execs and finance people didn’t think “hey, this will do terribly, but let’s make it anyway”

The movie itself was mid at best, I agree there. But I think I see what Favreau was going for. From the low budget titles to the complete lack of any kind of theme or depth to the cutesy stuff, I think they were going for a homage to classic movies. 

And I think that in part because it seemed to have a lot of homage: the Hutt planet was Blade Runner, the salt place was Hard Boiled, the arena was Star Trek.

I have to think it’s intentional, because there was a lot of it.

## 4. Could The Room Be Done Well?

**Score:** 33
**Body:** Recently a trailer for Bob Odenkirk’s version of Tommy Wiseau’s *The Room* popped up online.  I originally thought the idea was to remake it with professional actors doing their best to make it a good movie, but I was wrong — Odenkirk played it as a comedy.  

I’m wondering if a good movie could be made from the script.  

Hold the dialogue and locations constant, but feel free to change anything else: lighting, camera angles, editing, of course acting.  

Could your cinema dream team make the script work?
